groups.checked_argument: The selecting potential appears only in multiplier ideals; the continuous weight and positive volume define the norm. Evaluation gives total mass r! N_m/m^r, including the zero space; gauge changes preserve the combined metric weight.

Uniform continuity controls the continuous weight on a fixed local ball; holomorphic submean bounds all sections. A general weighted compact set still requires its explicit Bernstein--Markov hypothesis.

The defining ideals are contained in those of the selector at every positive real weight. Two envelope bounds give a bounded difference from P_I[phi] and hence I-equivalence; Choquet maxima preserve the quasi-everywhere obstacle after regularization.

Nested competitor families give monotonicity and translation. Concavity uses the multiplier-ideal inclusion for convex combinations, with the polar exceptional sets removed; smooth gauge changes are bijections of competitors.

The extremal formula gives the obstacle bound without N_m. Local Jacobian Lelong losses are O(1/m) on each fixed modification. The global envelope of the restricted obstacle transfers the K inequality to L1 limits; Hartogs controls the full upper limit.

Differentiating the Gram determinant gives the kernel measure. Orthogonal projection expresses the second derivative as a negative sum of squared norms; equality makes a real holomorphic quotient constant on connected X.
Positive kernel measures have exact total mass r!N_m/m^r. The determinant Lipschitz bound has this same constant, so both vanish under N_m=o(m^r).
Compressed multiplication has a convergent complex Neumann inverse for m norm(f)<log(3/2). Riesz evaluation yields holomorphic finite-degree densities and measures, including the common zero set.

Ordered compositions and complete Bell polynomials give the inverse derivatives. Gevrey bounds absorb ordered-product counts and factorials on a compact parameter interval; constants still depend on m.

The logarithmic derivative is m times the difference between coherent expectation and point value. The disk example is analytic pointwise in its parameter, but its norm perturbation is discontinuous and its center kernel has a cusp.
Orthogonality gives both marginals of the symmetric squared-kernel probability. Jensen gives contraction, symmetry gives selfadjointness, and a finite Gram expansion gives positivity.
The Markov derivative has zero mass and norm at most m osc(q)/2. Positivity sharpens set probabilities to logistic differential bounds, giving TV at most 2 tanh(m osc(weight difference)/4).

A one-dimensional constant space with smooth cap approximations reaches the sharp supremum. Normalizing the Neumann density gives complex radius log(3/2) and TV bound three independently of dimension.
On P1 times Y, weights q(y)/m tend uniformly to zero but leave distinct conditional Y probabilities in the limit. Thus uniform weight convergence cannot replace m times oscillation convergence.

Pullback preserves ideal order under the adjoint Jacobian formula and gives the same full-space continuous-obstacle competitors. Nonpluripolar locality off the exceptional set and increasing tests yield the pushforward identity even at infinite mass.

The relative canonical Jacobian metric from two smooth volumes gives an exact change-of-variables norm identity. Pullback times J identifies sections; kernels and measures push down in every normalization degree.

The cited compact Kahler theorem applies upstairs with the fixed relative canonical auxiliary bundle and positive selector mass. Its finite nonzero mass and determinant primitive are pushed down; these hypotheses are not consequences of the general Jacobian identities.

Compact connected fibers force section coefficients to be constant; local submersion sections give holomorphic descent. Probability fiber integration makes the norm isometric and transfers weak base limits, with degree dim B and zero ambient-degree limit.

The fiber probability has coefficient 1/2 and omega^n has coefficient 2n, giving 1/(2n) times the extended Hermitian MA lift. This gives a nonzero lower-degree limit in the stated Hopf threefold example without bounded upper mass.

Extending an orthonormal basis gives a positive kernel difference with mass exactly the codimension. An isolated n-dimensional pole requires max(floor(ma)-n+1,0) base order; points over one base point impose the largest order, and the jet quotient needs no surjectivity.

Bounded differences of base jet orders cost O(m^(q-1)); positive-mass Kahler base limits transfer. Moving a pole along a fiber changes stalk ideals while all selected spaces and kernels remain unchanged.
Projective monomial norms follow from Gaussian polar integration. Multinomial grouping gives D_m times the binomial tail at max(floor(ma)-q,0); the excluded count is binomial(r_m+q-1,q).

Entropy estimates give the tail logarithmic rate uniformly away from the image point; a selected terminal monomial gives global logarithmic domination for L1. Variance and the radial volume density q t^(q-1) give TV convergence away from the null level t=a.

The two radial branches match first derivatives and have rank q-1 inside the contact sphere, with no sphere measure. Line maximum principles give the largest dominated competitor; analytic singularity comparison identifies the ideal envelope, and descent gives the 2n mass factor.

All 38 figure source lines and all plotted coordinates were read; the original rendered figure was viewed. Seven finite-degree/limit curves are numerically reconstructed at all 2107 points with independent six-decimal rounding of both coordinates.

Removing constant and real-linear local metric terms leaves a uniform quadratic bound on m^(-1/2) balls. Evaluation targets one dimension, so summing an orthonormal basis introduces no extra dimension factor; integration gives O(m^d).

The r+1 normal-variable ideal threshold becomes max(floor(mc)-r,0) for a pulled-back coefficient, compared with floor(mc) on the divisor. Boundedly many restrictions cost O(m^(q-1)); the projective product example attains this order.

Nested kernel and determinant comparisons give O(1/m) normalized error. A positive residual gives a positive-mass reference to which the compact Kahler theorem applies; the general fixed-fiber-selector problem remains open.
Angle integration and x_j=norm(variable)^(2 power) reduce to a simplex radial integral. Integrability is strict: (ell+1)/p+sum(1/b_j)>P; equality diverges logarithmically.

A global lower bound includes the reference spaces, and one generic chart with a unit coefficient forces the upper order floor(mc-a). Floor differences are at most ceil(a); restriction counts give O(m^(q-1)), with the stated point bound when q=1.

Finite compact charts give a global divisorial lower bound. The strict threshold gives integrability in every model chart, with local boundedness elsewhere; the product constructions satisfy the chosen Hermitian curvature and positive residual for small coefficient.
For p=2,b=3,c=1/2, floor differences are one for m>=2. Polynomial dimensions give the displayed exact binomial defect and mass 2^(-q).

Normal-crossing integrability separates at intersections under the global lower bound; the generic upper charts are only required away from crossings. Finite-family metric estimates control simultaneous twists, and boundedly many restrictions give the summed shift bound.
Separate base/fiber variable pairs allow Fubini at crossings. The residual has mass q!/2^q, exact product section counts yield the claimed defect, and the selector remains non-descending.

The submersion fiber product is smooth, with relative Jacobian pulled from the modified base. The adjoint transform includes the Jacobian in the vanishing order; fixed canonical twists fit the restriction bound. Positive residual data yield a descended reference and pushforward mass.
Blowup Jacobian z^(q-1) converts exceptional orders into point-jet orders. The embedding into Pq times P(q-1) gives a positive residual, and exceptional intersection numbers give mass 1-2^(-q).

All order and restriction arguments remain valid for beta>=0 with a separately positive top integral. Exceptional fixed components can make selected and reference spaces coincide, even when a contracted line obstructs a positive smooth gauge.
The fixed exceptional order em leaves a point order max(floor(m(c-e)-a),0). The reference mass is k^q-delta^q, the critical count has degree q-1, and exact eventual vanishing is m(c-e-k)>=a+1.

Products of separating affine linear factors realize jets when the sum of orders is at most d+1. Two disjoint exceptional centers give positive semipositive mass 2^q-2 and exact defect 2 binomial(m+q-2,q-1), while the strict transform line has zero residual integral.

A radial weight tangent to the divisor-asymptotic branch is psh and largest by line maximum principles. Restriction to the selecting section and the global divisorial domination identify the total-space envelope.

Binomial modes give a global lower bound, Stirling ratios give the matching entropy rate, and monotonicity gives local uniform convergence. The beta radial density and null contact level give TV convergence for the reference norm.

Full evaluation sections concentrate pointwise; the compressed weighted norm is boundedly invertible. On the contact interior this gives B_weighted=B_reference/w+o(m^q). Dominated convergence identifies the base measure and keeps conditional fiber probabilities in its lift.
Radial integration gives exact Gamma monomial norms, complete Parseval bases, compact derivative convergence and fixed-scale tail collapse for growing orders.
Gamma-ratio moment bounds and Chebyshev give an L1 weight error O(T^(-1/2)). Grouping degrees by residues gives a threshold-uniform comparison with ordinary Poisson tails.

The first selected monomial determines the interior potential; compact density bounds give local TV convergence. Matching radial derivatives removes circle mass, leaving the pole atom outside the nonpluripolar measure. The Poisson central limit gives Gaussian transition for every growing order.

The metric remainder is negligible when q R tends to zero. Truncated Gamma norms agree uniformly below a fixed multiple of q, and monotonic radial moment ratios control the higher tail without a dimension loss.

Model trial polynomials concentrate locally. A fixed-annulus cutoff source is exponentially small; anticanonical twisting and a regularized logarithmic weight supply positive curvature and a vanishing-preserving correction. Weak compactness and the local selected evaluation bound give the matching lower limit.

The negative Fourier modes and real constant equation have an invertible Banach-space linearization. Stokes removes the imaginary constant. Matching boundary value/gradient yields a positive interior gap, a psh patched obstacle and uniqueness by the maximum principle; fixed-order Holder branches agree.

A bounded scale-R weight restores curvature inside the obstacle hole; q/R^2 absorbs its negative cutoff curvature outside. The singular weighted L2 estimate gives a linear correction with factor R^2/q and order q, including exterior sources approaching the zero-area boundary.

Polynomial chart truncations with fixed high smoothness control errors despite lack of exterior holomorphic extension. Positive-mode ring norms give Gaussian Riemann sums; relative Gram-form tails and order-preserving correction give the lower bound with no span dimension factor.

Signed normal distance converts the ring argument to 2 sqrt(m rho) d. Local full-density localization and selected obstacle correction prove saturation outside; restriction to an exterior half-band proves saturation inside. All limits retain q tending to infinity and q=o(m).

The graph displacement O(R^2) is negligible exactly when sqrt(q) R tends to zero for all data. A holomorphic coordinate change on a compact radial metric gives the sharp example; fixed-data necessity uses maximal displacement and boundary saturation.

First-order boundary matching gives b1=-((2r+1)-Lambda)P/(4r^2). Higher coefficients are determined recursively; finite truncations require sqrt(q) R^(J+1) tending to zero. A flat radial term has all Taylor coefficients zero but affects orders m/log m.

Splitting a at t^(-2/3) and t^(-1/3) isolates (log t)/(3t); the two tails and model replacement errors have the stated orders. Rotational monomial orthogonality makes the fixed-point kernel the inverse of one global norm, with FS leading constant 3/2.

Orthogonal product monomials turn total-order selection into a sum of independent index variables. One-factor radial transitions give convergence in distribution; centering/scales are not asserted to be exact moments. Fixed-radius Laplace bounds and total masses give global TV convergence.

Positive Taylor corrections give the largest-exponent critical growth and saturation. The isolated selector varies with m, has ideal m_p^k in total dimension q+f, and selects the same base jets isometrically only for the matched pushed-forward volume; fixed singularities and arbitrary base volumes remain outside this model.

Angular averaging of section growth separates all coefficients. Strict convexity and coercivity make the gradient a diffeomorphism. Angular maximum of a general psh competitor is convex with slopes in Q, so convex duality identifies the growth envelope; this is not an ideal-envelope identification.

An integral affine offset avoids parity loss. Fundamental-cell counting gives degree-d mass and O(1/m) slope-grid approximation; local Laplace bounds give logarithmic potential error and the Bernstein--Markov inequality.

Normalized monomials concentrate uniformly at inverse-gradient tori. Lattice Riemann sums give the shell measure. The C11 envelope Hessian has rank at most d; bounded mollified minors identify its products. Only in full dimension does the top product coincide with the shell measure.

Divisorial floors give one even and two odd first-factor monomials. Restriction to P1 fibers exhausts curvature by two half-atoms and identifies the full ideal envelope. Beta monomial measures concentrate on the unit circle, with two different leading masses despite potential convergence.

At each surface pole the ideal order is max(floor(t)-1,0). Lelong bounds and radial convexity give ordinary domination. Restriction to rational pencil curves exhausts their curvature, and a transverse curve identifies all competitors without torus-invariance assumptions.

The Gaussian obstacle on the compact sampling set reduces to s^2/4 on the pencil base; two maximum principles identify the piecewise envelope. Pole orders select |a-b|<=1 and 3m+1 monomials, a nonmultiplicative family; Gaussian norm bounds prove BM.

Diagonal grid monomials give a global lower bound; off-diagonal estimates give an integrable logarithmic pole error. Potentials converge locally and in every finite Lp, with uniform exponential convergence despite an unbounded difference near poles. Three Gaussian bands give probability shell limit and mass three; the top MA product remains zero.
